title: The Feast of Invisible Delicacies (ZH)
summary: Birbal settles an old score with a stingy noble who invited poor musicians to a 'feast of praises' without serving food.
full_text:
A wealthy nobleman named Nawab Shaukat Ali hired a troupe of wandering musicians to perform at his daughter's wedding. The musicians played their sitars and drums for six hours, entertaining hundreds of guests.

When the performance concluded, the musicians bowed, exhausted and hungry, asking for their payment and dinner.

The arrogant nobleman laughed mockingly: 'Payment? Food? Did you not hear the deafening applause of my guests? Did you not hear me shout "Wah! Wah! Subhanallah!" at your melodies?

'My applause was your payment! My royal praises were your feast! Praise is the highest food for artists; be on your way!'

The heartbroken musicians brought their grievance to Birbal.

A week later, Birbal invited Nawab Shaukat Ali to a private business meeting in the palace gardens to discuss a lucrative trade contract with the royal treasury. The nobleman arrived in his finest robes, bowing with deep respect.

Birbal sat the nobleman down and said: 'Nawab Sahib, I have prepared a grand imperial payment for your services.'

Birbal picked up an empty velvet pouch, opened the drawstring, and pointed into the empty air:

'Look inside this pouch, Nawab Sahib! Do you see these magnificent, sparkling diamonds from Golconda? Do you see these flawless emeralds? Feel their smooth weight!'

The nobleman looked into the empty pouch in bewilderment: 'My lord, there is nothing in this pouch! It is completely empty!'

Birbal looked at the nobleman with a radiant, theatrical smile:

'Did you not hear me praise the diamonds, Nawab Sahib? Did you not hear me shout "Wah! Wah! What brilliant gems!"?

'Just as your empty praises fed the starving musicians at your daughter's wedding, so too do my empty words pay for your services today!

'If spoken words are food for artists, then spoken words are gold for merchants! Take your bag of words and be on your way!'

The nobleman turned bright red with burning shame. Realizing his cruelty had been reflected back upon his own face, he dropped to his knees, apologized, and sent one hundred gold mohurs and a cartload of grain to the musician troupe immediately.

Akbar commended Birbal for teaching the court that honest labor must always be repaid with honest coin.
